I fixed the bug: `{% set full.prev_id, full.id = full.id, full.id + "/" + id %}` now works. The full test suite passes (910 tests), and the template from the issue renders `/a`, `/a/b`, `/a/b/c` as expected.

**Cause:** there were two problems.
- **Parser:** `parse_assign_target` only recognized `ns.attr` when it was the whole target. In a comma-separated target, each item was parsed as a plain name, so parsing stopped at the `.`.
- **Compiler:** the code for an `ns.attr` target inserted its "is this really a namespace?" check right in the middle of the assignment line. That only worked when there was a single target; with several targets it would produce invalid Python.

**Changes:**
- `src/jinja2/parser.py`:
  - `parse_primary` takes a new optional `with_namespace` flag and returns a namespace reference when it sees `name.attr`.
  - `parse_tuple` passes the flag on to each item, so namespace targets can sit anywhere in a list of targets.
  - `parse_assign_target` now relies on those two instead of its own one-off check. Nothing else passes the flag, so `for` loops and other targets behave as before.
- `src/jinja2/compiler.py`: a new helper, `_check_namespace_targets`, writes the namespace check for every `ns.attr` in the target before the assignment line. Both normal `set` and the block form (`{% set ns.x %}...{% endset %}`) use it. For the block form, the check still runs after the block body, as it did before.
- `tests/test_core_tags.py`: four new tests:
  - assigning two namespace attributes at once
  - swapping `ns.a, ns.b = ns.b, ns.a` (checks the right-hand side is evaluated before anything is assigned)
  - mixing a plain variable and a namespace attribute inside a loop, as in the issue
  - the "non-namespace object" error when one of the targets isn't a namespace
- `CHANGES.rst`: a changelog entry under 3.1.5. I left out an issue number because I didn't know the right one, so you may want to add it.

Nested parenthesized targets such as `(ns.a, b), c` are still rejected, same as before. I couldn't run mypy because it isn't installed in `.venv`. Nothing is committed.
